summary: This informational document presents a high-level architecture for building data-center network virtualization over Layer 3. It describes the major components of such a system and aims to divide the problem into smaller pieces that can be implemented separately.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes the main parts of an architecture for virtual networks in data centers. Tenant traffic travels through tunnels over a shared IP network, while control components keep track of where systems are connected.

subtitle: A high-level architecture for virtual networks over a data-center IP network.

tldr.problem: Data centers need to provide separate virtual networks while sharing physical infrastructure and allowing tenant systems to move.
tldr.mechanism: Network Virtualization Edges encapsulate tenant traffic across the IP underlay, while a Network Virtualization Authority provides mapping information to NVEs.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8014 is an Informational architecture overview. It identifies component interfaces and protocol work areas without specifying a single implementation.

today: RFC 8014 is an Informational architecture document published in December 2016. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Virtual Networks on Shared Infrastructure
sections.content:
NVO3 provides virtual networks to tenant systems by tunneling traffic across a data center's IP network. This decouples the network seen by a tenant from the physical network used to carry packets.

The architecture divides the system into components with clear interfaces so that parts can be implemented independently. A virtual network can provide Layer 2 service, Layer 3 service, or combined service.
sections.plainLanguage: Tenants use their own virtual networks on shared data-center equipment. Tunnels carry their packets across the shared IP network.

sections.title: NVEs, VAPs, and Tenant Interfaces
sections.content:
A Network Virtualization Edge (NVE) implements overlay functions at the boundary between tenant systems and the underlay. It encapsulates outgoing tenant traffic, removes the tunnel header from incoming traffic, and keeps local state for each virtual network it serves.

A Tenant System Interface connects to the NVE through a Virtual Access Point (VAP), a logical port associated with a virtual network. An NVE may run in a hypervisor, be split between a server and an adjacent switch, or be implemented in another network device.
sections.plainLanguage: The NVE is the edge that wraps and unwraps tenant packets. Each tenant connection reaches a virtual network through a logical port called a VAP.

sections.title: Layer 2 and Layer 3 Services
sections.content:
For Layer 2 service, the NVE forwards Ethernet frames based on tenant MAC addresses, and the virtual network behaves like an Ethernet network. For Layer 3 service, the NVE forwards IP packets based on IP addresses and ignores tenant-supplied Layer 2 destination addresses.

A combined service provides Layer 2 behavior within a virtual network and IP processing for traffic entering or leaving it. The RFC notes that an NVO3 virtual network presents an Ethernet interface to the tenant system in either service model.
sections.plainLanguage: Layer 2 service carries Ethernet frames, while Layer 3 service routes IP packets. A deployment can combine both kinds of service.

sections.title: Mapping Tenant Addresses to NVEs
sections.content:
Before forwarding traffic to a remote tenant system, an NVE needs to know the remote NVE's address. A Network Virtualization Authority (NVA) provides address mappings and other information to NVEs.

The NVA can learn mappings from a VM orchestration system or directly from NVEs when tenant systems attach or detach. An NVE may subscribe to information for only the virtual networks it serves and may query for an individual mapping when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The NVA keeps track of which NVE serves each tenant address. An NVE can request or subscribe to the mappings it needs.

sections.title: Gateways, Federation, and Operations
sections.content:
Gateways connect virtual networks to external networks, legacy systems, or other virtual networks. Cross-network traffic is controlled by policy. Distributed inter-VN gateways let NVEs forward directly when they have the required policy information, reducing paths that detour through a central gateway.

Separate NVAs can exchange mappings for virtual networks shared across administrative domains. The architecture also calls for operational tools to diagnose faults that may be hidden by the overlay's abstraction of the underlay.
sections.plainLanguage: Gateways provide controlled paths between virtual networks and other networks. When multiple domains share a virtual network, their NVAs exchange the needed mapping information.
